lesson.title: The Man That Knows
lesson.subtitle: qui for the subject after the gap (l'homme qui parle), que for the object (le café que je veux).

hook.title: qui vs. que: The One-Second Look-Ahead Test
hook.content: Look at the very first word AFTER the gap: (1) Is it a VERB (parle, arrive, est)? Drop in qui (and NEVER elide qui, even before a vowel!). (2) Is it a SUBJECT PRONOUN or NOUN (je, tu, il, Marie)? Drop in que (or qu' before a vowel)!

footnotes.title: Why qui never drops its -i before a vowel, whereas que always drops its -e
footnotes.content: To keep subject (qui) and object (qu') distinct, qui NEVER elides (l'homme qui arrive), while que ALWAYS elides before a vowel (le train qu'il prend)!

pattern.title: Gap + Verb → qui; Gap + Subject → que / qu'
pattern.content: Run the one-second look-ahead test across people and things alike.
pattern.linguist_note: Case-marked relativizers qui (nominative) and que (accusative) preserve syntactic role transparency.
pattern.trap_note: Never elide qui (*l'ami qu'arrive) and never omit que (*le livre je lis)!

exercises.prompt: Apply the look-ahead test to match each sentence with qui or que/qu':

matching_pairs.english: Le train ___ arrive (+ vowel verb arrive)
matching_pairs.german: qui (Le train qui arrive — never elides!)

matching_pairs.english: Le café ___ je prends (+ subject je)
L'ami ___ il invite (+ vowel subject il)

exercises.target_answer: qui (La femme qui parle), qui (Le train qui arrive — never elides!), que (Le café que je prends), qu' (L'ami qu'il invite — que elides!)
exercises.meaning: La femme ___ parle (+ verb parle), Le train ___ arrive (+ vowel verb arrive), Le café ___ je prends (+ subject je), L'ami ___ il invite (+ vowel subject il)
exercises.explanation: Look one word to the right: Verb → qui; Subject → que / qu'.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two blanks: 'C'est un ami ___ habite à Paris et ___ j'aime beaucoup':
exercises.meaning: Before verb habite → qui; before subject j' → que
exercises.explanation: habite is a verb (qui); j'aime has subject j' (que).

exercises.prompt: Combine 'Voici le gâteau' + 'Je veux le gâteau' into 'Voici le gâteau ___ je veux':
exercises.target_answer: Voici le gâteau que je veux
exercises.meaning: Here is the cake that I want
exercises.explanation: Because subject je follows the gap, use que: Voici le gâteau que je veux.

exercises.idea: the restaurant that is here is very good
cues: The restaurant that is here (+ verb est!) → Le restaurant qui est ici
is very good → est très bon
idea_parts: head noun + subject relative → Le restaurant qui est ici
exercises.target_answer: Le restaurant qui est ici est très bon
exercises.meaning: The restaurant that is here is very good
exercises.explanation: Because the verb est follows the gap, use qui.

diagnosis.cue: Things take qui whenever they are the subject of the following verb!

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: C'est le film qu'elle a vu hier
exercises.target_answer: C'est le film qu'elle a vu hier
exercises.meaning: That is the movie she saw yesterday
exercises.explanation: que elides before vowel-initial subject elle: qu'elle a vu.
exercises.affirmation: You wrote qu'elle with the elided object relative!

summary.outcome: Select qui vs. que/qu' instantaneously by checking whether a verb or a subject follows the gap.

use_example.german: Le train qui part maintenant est le train que je voulais prendre.
use_example.english: The train that is leaving now is the train that I wanted to take.

summary.takeaway: Verb after the gap → qui (never elides); Subject after the gap → que / qu' (never omitted).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2802] Que Everywhere): see how The Man That Knows leads directly into Que Everywhere.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "The restaurant that is here is very good" in French:
twist.target_answer: Le restaurant qui est ici est très bon
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Le restaurant qui est ici est très bon" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Man That Knows.

qui.context_phrase: L'homme qui parle est mon père.
qui.context_translation: The man who is speaking is my father.
qui.etymology_derivation: Followed directly by the verb. Never drops its i before a vowel!

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

homme.etymology_derivation: Latin homō 'man' — the root of human, homicide, humus (of the earth). The H is written and never said.

ville.etymology_derivation: Latin vīlla 'country estate' grew into the whole city in French (leaving 'city' as la cité for the historic core).

train.context_phrase: Le train part à huit heures.
train.etymology_derivation: Old French traïn 'a line of things pulled along'.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

aimé.etymology_derivation: aimer ← ad + estimare 'to estimate'. English 'aim' drifted from the same estimate — aiming is assessing.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
